Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

prince noun

also crown prince, king’s son

classical

Liv. 1.46.4: Prīscī Tarquinī rēgis fīlius
Cic. Amic. 70: rēgum fīliī

rēgis fīlius

noun phrase: fīlius with the genitive rēgis

a king’s son, a prince

Latin says it with a phrase. The heir to the throne is rēgnī hērēs (M-O s.v. king: heir apparent).

Other words

  • rēgulus, rēgulī m. — a king’s son; more often a petty king

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Liv. 42.24.10 (Lewis & Short); Liv. 45.14.6 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. prince

    Livy’s word for Masinissa’s sons; most often the ruler of a small people, a chieftain (Sall., Liv., Tac.), and not found in Caesar or Cicero (Lewis & Short).

  • puer rēgius — the king’s boy, a young prince

    noun phrase: puer with the adjective rēgius · also used · classical · Verg. A. 1.677 (Lewis & Short, s.v. rēgius)

    Vergil’s phrase for the young Ascanius.

  • prīnceps, prīncipis m. — a ruling prince

    noun, third declension · also used · Renaissance · M-O s.v. prince; Levi–Bini p. 4

    Classically the first man in the state, and from Augustus on the emperor (see emperor). Vives (1540) uses it for the ruler of a principality, and Levi and Bini say that a prince can be addressed in Latin only as prīnceps.

Examples

  • ut in fābulīs, quī aliquamdiū propter ignōrātiōnem stirpis et generis in famulātū fuērunt, cum cognitī sunt et aut deōrum aut rēgum fīliī inventī, retinent tamen cāritātem in pāstōrēs, quōs patrēs multōs annōs esse dūxērunt

    as in stories: those who, not knowing their birth and family, have lived for a while as servants, and then are recognised and found to be the sons of gods or kings, still keep their love for the shepherds they took for their fathers for many yearsCic. Amic. 70

See also king, queen, princess, palace, castle.
